docsPage.lede: What Freally OS keeps, why it has no network yet, and how to check that an image is ours.
docsPage.network.p1: Freally OS can't make network connections yet. It has no network driver and no network stack: they arrive later on the road to 1.0, and the update check will ask before it ever connects.
docsPage.network.p2: You can check it yourself: start it in a virtual machine with a network adapter, and watch the host's traffic for that machine (Wireshark will do). It sends nothing.
docsPage.network.title: The network
docsPage.privacy.p1: Freally OS collects nothing. There is no telemetry, no crash upload, no account with us and no background connection: none of it was ever written.
docsPage.privacy.p2: Your accounts and files stay on your computer, each account's home encrypted with a key only its password opens.
docsPage.privacy.p3: The hardware report in Settings is text you can read before you send it, and it goes only where you send it.
docsPage.privacy.p4: The tester sign-up, when it opens, keeps an email address and nothing else, only for the tester programme, and deletes it when you ask.
docsPage.privacy.p5: This site loads nothing from other sites and runs no analytics.
docsPage.privacy.title: Privacy
docsPage.verify.p1: Every official image is built from the public source, and the build is reproducible: the same commit gives the same bootloader and the same image, byte for byte, apart from the image's signature.
docsPage.verify.p2: To check one, check out the version's tag, run cargo xtask hashes --unsigned, and compare the two SHA-256 sums on its release line (the bootloader's, and the image's with its signature left out) with the ones published beside the image. They must be equal.
docsPage.verify.p3: Then the signature: the bootloader refuses any image not signed by a key it trusts, and says so on the screen. A changed byte anywhere in the image is caught before Freally OS starts.
docsPage.verify.title: Checking an official image
featuresPage.coming.downloads: There are no downloads before version 1.0, and none on this page.
featuresPage.coming.intro: Stated plainly. Freally OS is built one version at a time, and most of it isn't built yet. Each version on the road to 1.0 is marked with its state.
featuresPage.coming.title: What is still coming
featuresPage.compare.asOf: Freally OS's column is version 1.0, which is not out yet. The other systems change too; this table is as of November 2026.
featuresPage.compare.intro: Freally OS 1.0 next to the desktop systems most people use, each as its maker ships it.
featuresPage.compare.note.admin: an administrator can change the system
featuresPage.compare.note.chromium: ChromiumOS is; ChromeOS adds closed parts
featuresPage.compare.note.layer: standard apps, through its own layer
featuresPage.compare.note.msAccount: setup asks for a Microsoft account
featuresPage.compare.row.anyPc: Runs on a PC you already own
featuresPage.compare.row.noAccount: Set up without an online account
featuresPage.compare.row.oneAuthor: Every line written by one author, to one charter
featuresPage.compare.row.sealed: A verified system that apps can't change
featuresPage.compare.summary: Only Freally OS is written entirely by one author, to one charter. That is what lets it explain every process and promise there is nothing in it from anyone else.
featuresPage.compare.theyWin: Windows, macOS, Ubuntu and ChromeOS run far more apps on far more hardware, today and at Freally OS 1.0. Freally OS trades that breadth for being consistent, quiet, sealed and explained.
featuresPage.compare.title: Next to the systems people use today
featuresPage.free.body: Freally OS is free today, for everyone: no paid tier, no subscription and no account. Its code is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
featuresPage.free.title: Free today
featuresPage.lede: What works today, and what Freally OS 1.0 will have.
featuresPage.limits.apps: It won't run every Windows or Mac app: standard ones, through its own layers.
featuresPage.limits.hardware: It runs on x86-64 computers it has drivers for, starting with one laptop.
featuresPage.limits.servers: It is a desktop system: not for servers or phones.
featuresPage.limits.title: What 1.0 does not do
featuresPage.numbers.ktests: kernel tests, run inside the kernel
featuresPage.numbers.specs: end-to-end checks on a running machine
featuresPage.today.accounts.body: The first start makes the owner's account; the password opens that person's home and nobody else's. An account moves to another computer as one sealed file.
featuresPage.today.accounts.title: Accounts that stay yours
featuresPage.today.boot.body: It reads the system image, checks its signature and every block, and shows why it refused one that fails.
featuresPage.today.boot.title: Its own bootloader
featuresPage.today.calculator.body: Exact decimals: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3, and a third shows 32 digits. Standard and scientific, typed or pressed, with a history.
featuresPage.today.calculator.title: Calculator
featuresPage.today.conductor.body: Conductor starts as process 1, from the signed image, in its own protected memory.
featuresPage.today.conductor.title: The first program
featuresPage.today.cores.body: Every processor core runs, each with its own queue, and one with nothing to do takes work from a busy one.
featuresPage.today.cores.title: Every core
featuresPage.today.desktop.body: The Rack along the bottom with app keys and a clock, a launcher on the Super key, and windows in light and dark.
featuresPage.today.desktop.title: The desktop
featuresPage.today.faults.body: A program that crashes ends alone and leaves a report. Even a kernel stop is reported when the computer next starts.
featuresPage.today.faults.title: Fault reports
featuresPage.today.files.body: Settings for your look, accounts, updates and a hardware report. Files for your home, with a bin, dragging between windows, and copies you can pause and check.
featuresPage.today.files.title: Settings and Files
featuresPage.today.kernel.body: Memory where nothing is both writable and runnable, interrupts and timers, a scheduler with four classes, and messages between programs.
featuresPage.today.kernel.title: Freally Core, the kernel
featuresPage.today.monitor.body: Every process and what it's for, the boot stage by stage, every crash and the log, on Super+M.
featuresPage.today.monitor.title: Monitor
featuresPage.today.storage.body: FreallyFS: copy-on-write, a checksum on every block, snapshots, and each home encrypted with its own key. Cut off mid-write 1,000 times in tests, it came back whole every time.
featuresPage.today.storage.title: Its own file system
featuresPage.today.swap.body: In developer builds a running service can be replaced, and put back, without a restart. Release builds don't carry it.
featuresPage.today.swap.title: Live swaps, for developers
featuresPage.today.terminal.body: A command line with its own shell: every process, the boot's times, the log and memory, a command away.
featuresPage.today.terminal.title: Terminal and Shell
featuresPage.today.title: What works today
featuresPage.today.updates.body: A signed update goes onto the half of the system that isn't running and starts on trial. If it doesn't start, the computer goes back to the version before by itself.
featuresPage.today.updates.title: Updates from a file
featuresPage.version: Every number on this page comes from the build that produced it. There is nothing to download before version 1.0.
featuresPage.why.apps.body: Each app runs in its own sandbox with only the permissions it was given. The system itself changes only with a new signed image.
featuresPage.why.apps.title: Apps can't change the system
featuresPage.why.open.body: The code is open source, and the builds are reproducible: build the official image yourself and check that it's identical.
featuresPage.why.open.title: Open and reproducible
featuresPage.why.ours.body: No library from outside the project, and a build check refuses one. The only exceptions are Rust's core library and the Noto fonts, both listed in the notices.
featuresPage.why.ours.title: Every line is its own
featuresPage.why.refused.body: Every official build is one signed image. Before anything in it runs, the bootloader checks the signature and every block. An image that fails is never run, and the screen says why.
featuresPage.why.refused.title: Signed or refused
featuresPage.why.title: Why it is built the way it is
footer.licence: Open source under the Apache License 2.0. © Mike Weaver. The Freally name, icons and look are not covered by the code's licence.
footer.yours: Your files and accounts stay on your computer. Freally OS sends nothing anywhere unless you ask it to.
hero.headline: A computer that's on your side.
hero.sub: Freally OS starts in seconds, runs only what you asked for, and every line of it is written in-house.
honest.downloads.body: No beta on this page, no preview build, no early access. Each version is built and tested in private until 1.0.
honest.downloads.title: There are no downloads before 1.0
honest.early.body: Freally OS runs on its author's own computers for now. It does very little yet that you would use every day, and the road above says plainly when each part arrives.
honest.early.title: It is early
honest.privacy.body: There is no telemetry, no crash upload, no account and no background connection. The update check, when it arrives, runs only when you turn it on, and tells you what it will download before it does. This site loads nothing from other sites and runs no analytics.
honest.privacy.title: It collects nothing
honest.title: The things most sites put at the bottom
ladder.intro: One line per version, in order. This is the same ladder the private plan follows: if one moves, both move, and a build check compares them.
ladder.note: A version that is done is built, tested and tagged. It is not a download: there are none, and there won't be until 1.0.
ladder.rung.v0.1.0: The foundation: its own bootloader checks a signed system image and paints the screen, and every quality check runs on every change.
ladder.rung.v0.11.5: Together: invite anyone, on any computer or phone, by a link or a QR code, to work with you in the apps you share.
ladder.rung.v0.12.0: Freally's own programming language, first version.
ladder.rung.v0.13.0: The app sandbox, and Freally Guard.
ladder.rung.v0.18.0: Pictures, your own background, and Photos.
ladder.rung.v0.2.0: Freally Core, the kernel: memory, interrupts, timers, a scheduler and messages. The first program starts, and a crash leaves a report.
ladder.rung.v0.20.0: The browser: the web without scripts.
ladder.rung.v0.27.0: Media: a player, a recorder and the camera.
ladder.rung.v0.3.0: Services and drivers: every processor core, the screen, keyboard and mouse, and updates that fall back on their own if they fail.
ladder.rung.v0.30.7: Mac programs: apps made only for Apple silicon.
ladder.rung.v0.31.0: The Freally music apps, with VST3 and CLAP plugins.
ladder.rung.v0.32.0: Every setting, every language, and a screen reader.
ladder.rung.v0.33.0: Install to the computer's own drive.
ladder.rung.v0.4.0: First light: the desktop, a terminal, a shell, and Monitor, which explains every process. The desktop in under 3 seconds.
ladder.rung.v0.5.0: The real laptop: Freally OS starts from a USB stick on its first laptop.
ladder.rung.v0.6.0: Developer tools: replace a running service in place, and roll it back, without a restart.
ladder.rung.v0.7.0: Storage, encrypted local accounts, Settings and Files.

ladder.rung.v1.0.0-rc.N: The release candidate: every feature tested on real hardware.
ladder.rung.v1.1.0 … v2.0.0: After 1.0: one version at a time.

promises.fast.body: The desktop in under 3 seconds, measured on every build. A change that breaks that budget doesn't ship.
promises.fast.title: Fast
promises.quiet.body: Nothing runs that you didn't start, and every process says in one sentence what it does.
promises.quiet.title: Quiet
promises.title: Three promises
promises.yours.body: No account, no cloud and no telemetry. Updates ask first, and every update can be undone.
promises.yours.title: Yours
site.tagline: A computer that's on your side.
what.p1: Freally OS is a new desktop operating system, written from the first instruction up: its own bootloader, kernel, drivers, desktop and apps, all in Rust, all in-house.
what.p2: Apart from Rust's core library, none of its code comes from another project. That is how it can promise what other systems offer only as settings: there is no telemetry to turn off, because none was ever written.
what.p3: It is early. Today it starts, checks its own signature, and runs its kernel and its first program. The road below shows every step to 1.0, in order.
what.title: What it is
